pages.title: Review the last lesson
pages.instruction: Imagine your team is considering a change to its weekly meeting. Help your teacher decide whether to try it

items.prompt: I’d like us to send written updates before our weekly meeting. What might worry the team?
items.hint: People might worry they’ll have to write an update and repeat it at the meeting
items.cue: Name a concern someone might raise about the change

items.prompt: How could I show I’ve understood that concern?
items.hint: It sounds as if you’re worried about doing the same work twice. Is that fair?
items.cue: Put the concern into words and give the team a chance to correct you

items.prompt: What could we try at our next meeting?
items.hint: We could use meeting time just for questions. Would you be willing to try that once?
items.cue: Suggest one adjustment and ask whether I would try it

pages.title: Read Laura’s feedback
pages.instruction: Answer the questions using Laura’s email. Find the detail that supports each answer
pages.subject: Laura’s email about Tuesday’s presentation
paragraphs: Hi Ana, Thank you and your team for the presentation Raj delivered on Tuesday. He really knows the project, and he has a friendly style. The slides had a lot of information. To be fair, there was a lot to say in thirty minutes.
Some of us found the second part a bit hard to understand, and we didn’t get an answer to my question about the deadline.
It might be worth meeting again next week, just for the important points. Would Thursday at ten work? It would be great if you could be there too.

questions.prompt: Which two qualities does Laura praise in Raj?
questions.answer: She praises his knowledge of the project and his friendly style.
questions.hint: Find what Laura says about his knowledge and the way he presents.

questions.answer: Laura’s question about the deadline was left unanswered.
questions.hint: Find the specific question mentioned in paragraph two.

questions.prompt: When does Laura suggest meeting again?
questions.answer: She suggests Thursday at ten next week.
questions.hint: Look for both the day and the time in the final paragraph.

questions.prompt: Besides Raj, whom does Laura ask to attend?
questions.answer: She asks Ana, the email’s recipient, to attend as well.
questions.hint: Laura is writing to Ana and says, “if you could be there too”.

pages.title: Practise the conversation
pages.instruction: You are Ana and Teacher is Kim. Practise together, swap roles, then answer the questions

lines.speaker: Kim
lines.text: So, the big talk with Raj is tomorrow?
lines.audioText: So, the big talk with Raj is tomorrow?
lines.translation: Então a grande conversa com o Raj é amanhã?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Yes. I’ll start with: “You really know the project, and I like your style.”
lines.audioText: Yes. I’ll start with: “You really know the project, and I like your style.”

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Then: “You talked too fast and just read the slides.”

lines.speaker: Kim
lines.text: Hmm. That sounds a bit harsh
lines.audioText: Hmm. That sounds a bit harsh.

questions.answer: Ana plans to say that Raj spoke too fast and read the slides

questions.answer: Ana will praise Raj’s knowledge of the project and his style
Kim thinks Ana’s criticism sounds a bit harsh

lines.speaker: Kim
lines.text: Sure, but it might come across as an attack. Try: “It seemed a little rushed.”
lines.audioText: Sure, but it might come across as an attack. Try: “It seemed a little rushed.”

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: “It seemed a little rushed.” And for the slides, maybe—
lines.audioText: “It seemed a little rushed.” And for the slides, maybe—

lines.speaker: Kim
lines.text: Maybe “The slides tend to—” Sorry, go on
lines.audioText: Maybe “The slides tend to—” Sorry, go on.

lines.audioText: No, that’s it! “The slides tend to have a lot of text. You might want to cut some.”

questions.prompt: How does Kim suggest softening the criticism?
questions.answer: Kim suggests describing the effect rather than making an accusation

questions.prompt: What phrase does Ana choose about the pace?
questions.answer: Ana chooses the phrase “It seemed a little rushed”

questions.prompt: What specific change does Ana suggest for the slides?
questions.answer: Ana suggests that Raj cut some text from the slides

pages.title: Discuss Laura’s feedback with Raj
pages.instruction: You are Ana; Teacher is Raj. Explain Laura’s feedback, invite his perspective and agree on a next step

items.prompt: What did Laura say about my presentation?
items.cue: Acknowledge what Laura praised, then explain the two specific concerns
items.hint: She valued your knowledge and friendly style. She found the second part hard to follow, and her deadline question wasn’t answered

items.prompt: There was a lot to cover in thirty minutes. What would you like to ask me?
items.cue: Ask Raj about a specific difficulty rather than assume why it happened
items.hint: Which part was hardest to fit into the time? What made the deadline question difficult to answer?

items.prompt: What could we do before meeting Laura again?
items.cue: Suggest one practical preparation step and check whether Raj agrees
items.hint: Could we choose the key points and prepare the deadline answer together? Would that help?

pages.title: Build cautious statements with seem, tend and might
pages.instruction: Use verb patterns and a modal to make a claim less absolute

rows.subject: An impression
rows.verb: seem + adjective / seem to + base verb
rows.example: The pace seems rushed. The slides seem to contain a lot of text

rows.subject: A tendency
rows.example: The introduction tends to run long

rows.subject: A possibility
rows.example: The comment might sound personal. It might be misunderstood

pages.note: Seem and tend take to before another verb; might does not. He/she/it seems or tends, but might has no -s ending. A cautious form still needs a clear reason.

pages.title: Make the feedback useful
pages.instruction: Give Raj specific feedback and agree on one practical next step

pages.title: Listen and answer
pages.instruction: Raj responds to the feedback. Listen for what he accepts and the point he wants to clarify
pages.message: Hi, Ana, it’s Raj. Thanks for today. Really. It was… constructive. I’ll take it on board. I guess I did talk a bit fast. But, to be fair, nobody told me Laura would ask about the deadline. I didn’t know how to handle it. And the slides were Sarah’s. I only saw them on Monday. Anyway. I’ll try not to rush next time. Oh, and Thursday? I wonder if I could talk to Laura directly. Just me. I think it’s worth trying. Let me know. Thanks
pages.audioText: Hi, Ana, it’s Raj. Thanks for today. Really. It was… constructive. I’ll take it on board. I guess I did talk a bit fast. But, to be fair, nobody told me Laura would ask about the deadline. I didn’t know how to handle it. And the slides were Sarah’s. I only saw them on Monday. Anyway. I’ll try not to rush next time. Oh, and Thursday? I wonder if I could talk to Laura directly. Just me. I think it’s worth trying. Let me know. Thanks.
pages.greeting: Can we talk about the presentation?

items.prompt: What does Raj accept about his delivery?
items.answer: Raj accepts that he rushed and says he will try not to rush next time

items.prompt: Who made the slides, and when did Raj see them?
items.answer: Sarah made the slides; Raj only saw them on Monday

items.prompt: How does Raj want to meet Laura on Thursday?
items.answer: Raj wants to speak to Laura alone

pages.title: Respond to the message
pages.instruction: Keep the reply constructive. Your teacher plays Raj. Respond to his concern and agree a workable arrangement

items.prompt: I’d prefer to meet Laura on my own
items.cue: Acknowledge the preference without promising a change
items.hint: I can see why you’d prefer to discuss the feedback privately

items.prompt: Why does Ana need to be there?
items.cue: Explain Laura’s request without sounding defensive
items.hint: Laura asked Ana to join so we can discuss the presentation together

items.prompt: Could we find an arrangement that works for both of us?
items.cue: Propose a specific compromise and check agreement
items.hint: Could Ana join for the presentation feedback, and then give you time alone with Laura? Would that work for you?

items.prompt: What behaviour does the blamethrower metaphor describe?
items.answer: It describes passing responsibility for your actions to other people

items.prompt: How does he distinguish dogmatism from a supported claim?
items.hint: Listen to the contrast between facts and opinions
items.answer: He describes dogmatism as presenting opinions as if they were facts

items.prompt: Why might exaggeration make a message less credible?
items.hint: Connect the exaggeration example to trust
items.answer: Example: If everything is described as extraordinary, the listener may stop trusting the strength of the claim

items.prompt: Give feedback on that habit without labelling the person
items.hint: Use tends to or comes across as, then invite a response
items.answer: Example: The message tends to sound certain before the evidence is clear. Could we make the level of confidence more explicit?
